   tolerance-based comparison is the correct instrument for
   a floating-point result.

4. **Two dialects.** Take the condensed GitHub Actions
   workflow shown in this chapter and translate it into the
   equivalent `.gitlab-ci.yml`. Identify the two structural
   differences between the dialects (jobs-and-steps versus
   stages-and-scripts, and per-file versus single-file
   configuration), and explain why single-sourcing the
   check logic in a `Makefile` would let both files shrink
   to a thin shim.

5. **Archetype and gates.** For each of the five archetypes
   (data analysis, manuscript, R package, simulation, blog),
   state which of the three CI gates apply and why. For the
   simulation archetype, describe specifically how you would
   arrange a reduced pipeline under CI and a full pipeline
   elsewhere, and what role a fixed seed plays in making the
   reduced run a genuine reproducibility test.

6. **Independent verification.** Read the CODECHECK
   description of Nust and Eglen [@nust2021codecheck].
   Explain in what respect an independent codechecker plays
   the same role, for a submitted analysis, that a CI runner
   plays for a committed change. Then identify one class of
   reproducibility failure that an independent human
   codechecker would catch and that the author's own CI,
   however well configured, cannot.

7. **Cumulative: gate the cohort compendium.** Using the
   pattern of 'Demonstrating a gate on the cohort
   compendium', run
   `used <- unique(renv::dependencies('R/cohort.R')$Package)`
   and compute
   `missing <- setdiff(used, c('tibble', 'ggplot2', 'stats', 'utils', rownames(installed.packages(priority = 'base'))))`.
   Report the length of `missing` (an autogradable answer:
   a single integer). Then add the line `library(sandwich)`
   to a copy of `R/cohort.R` on disk, re-run the same two
   lines against the copy, and report the exact character
   vector `missing` now contains (a second autogradable
   answer: one package name, spelled exactly as it would
   appear in a real CI log).

8. **Spacing: commit before you compute, revisited.** This
   exercise returns to the commit discipline of Chapter 4
   (@sec-version-control). A CI workflow triggers on
   `push`, so it can only test what has actually been
   committed; any undeclared state that exists solely in
   an uncommitted file or an author's working directory is
   invisible to it in exactly the way it is invisible to a
   colleague who clones the repository. Explain, in your
   own words, why this makes 'commit before you compute'
   (habit 1) a precondition for CI to mean anything at all,
   and give one concrete example of an uncommitted change
   that would let a build pass locally and fail the moment
   it is pushed.

## Solutions

Attempt an exercise before expanding its solution. Exercises
3 and 4 are hands-on and their outputs will vary; the boxes
record the expected result and the reasoning.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 1

The ladder grades **capture**: how far down the determinant
stack a result is locked. CI locks nothing. It installs no
package into the lockfile and no library into the image, so
removing it leaves every pinned layer exactly as pinned as
before. A compendium at L2 with CI and the same compendium
at L2 without it sit on the same rung.

**What is lost is assurance rather than level.** Without CI
nobody rebuilds the captured environment on a clean machine
and re-runs the analysis in it. The compendium becomes
trusted rather than tested, and the distance between 'this
should rebuild' and 'this does rebuild' stops being
measured.

**A concrete failure.** A base image is repointed by its
maintainer and the Dockerfile pins it by tag rather than
digest, so the environment quietly changes underneath the
project. With CI, the next push rebuilds and the check
fails, naming the day it broke. Without CI, the compendium
looks healthy on the author's machine, where an old image
is cached locally, and fails for the first reader who
builds it from scratch, possibly years later, with no
indication of when or why it broke. Equally good answers:
a package pulled from CRAN and no longer restorable, a
system library the analysis silently depended on and never
declared, or a chunk that only ever ran because of state
left in the author's session.

The general shape of the loss is that decay is silent and
CI is what makes it loud.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

**`R CMD check`** catches a defect in the package skin as
code: a function in `R/` calling a package that is used but
not declared in `DESCRIPTION` (a WARNING, so the gate must
fail on warnings), a syntax error in a file under `R/` that
nothing currently calls, a documented argument that no
longer exists. The render gate would not see it if the
report does not touch that function, and the manifest gate
checks declarations rather than whether the code loads.
The same defects under `analysis/` are invisible to
`R CMD check`, which never sees that directory.

**The render gate** catches a defect that appears only when
the document is built: a chunk that fails on a clean
machine because it read an uncommitted file, a figure whose
code errors, a cross-reference to a label that no longer
exists. `R CMD check` never renders, so it sees none of
this.

**The dependency-manifest gate** catches drift between the
three manifests: a package used in the code and absent
from `DESCRIPTION`, or declared in `DESCRIPTION` and
missing from `renv.lock`. The code may load and the
document may render perfectly on a machine where the
package happens to be installed, so neither other gate
fires.

**A failure none of the three catches:** a change in the
*data*. A raw extract silently replaced with a corrected
version leaves the code valid, the document renderable,
and the manifests consistent, while every number in the
report changes. All three gates pass. The **data-integrity
gate** addresses it, by hashing the inputs and derived
outputs and comparing against a recorded manifest.

The **verification gate** addresses the adjacent case in
which the code changes a result without any of the three
noticing, by comparing computed outputs against recorded
baselines.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 3

```r
library(digest)
m1 <- lm(outcome ~ arm, data = cohort)
d1 <- digest(coef(m1), algo = 'sha256')

m2 <- lm(outcome ~ arm, data = cohort)
digest(coef(m2), algo = 'sha256') == d1     # TRUE

cohort$outcome[1] <- cohort$outcome[1] + 1
m3 <- lm(outcome ~ arm, data = cohort)
digest(coef(m3), algo = 'sha256') == d1     # FALSE
```

Refitting the identical model to identical data, in the
same session, gives an identical digest; altering one
outcome value changes it (verified above: `TRUE` then
`FALSE`, on R 4.6.1).

**Why the digest is sensitive to any change.** The
coefficients are a deterministic function of the data and
the model specification. Nothing about the time of
fitting, the machine's fonts, or the session's history
enters them, so within one session and platform the digest
changes exactly when a number changes and not otherwise.

**Why it is still the wrong tool for verification.** A
digest compares serialized *bytes*, not numeric *values*.
R's own documentation for `serialize()` (the mechanism
`digest()` and `saveRDS()` both rely on) states that the
default serialization format changed from version 2 to
version 3 in R 3.6.0, and warns explicitly that 'the
serialization format may change in future versions of R, so
this interface should not be used for long-term storage of
R objects' (`?serialize`, inspected). Nothing guarantees
that two R versions, or two platforms, serialize an
identical numeric vector to identical bytes; an added
attribute, a changed internal representation, or a future
format bump can flip the digest while every coefficient is
still correct to the last bit. That makes a coefficient
digest a plausible false-positive generator across
upgrades, exactly the failure mode this book's baseline
test is built to avoid by comparing *values* with
`expect_equal(..., tolerance = ...)` rather than comparing
serialized bytes with `==`. The digest in @tbl-integrity is
defensible because it targets the raw data bytes on disk,
where byte-for-byte identity is the actual requirement;
reused on a fitted model's coefficients, it answers a
different, stricter question ('are the bytes identical')
than the one a reproducibility check needs answered ('is
the value the same within tolerance'), and will occasionally
answer it wrong in a way that looks like a false alarm.

One practical refinement the exercise invites. Digesting
the whole `lm` object rather than `coef()` is fragile,
because the object stores the call and a `terms`
environment, which can carry incidental references. Hashing
the coefficient vector, or a named list of the quantities
actually reported, is more robust against incidental
differences, but does not remove the cross-version risk
above; a baseline test with a stated tolerance remains the
right tool for verifying that an estimate has not drifted.

**Why hashing a plot would not be sound.** A rendered plot
is an image file, and image files embed creation
timestamps, are affected by device version and font
availability, and can differ in their compression between
runs. Two plots of the identical model can differ byte for
byte while depicting exactly the same thing, so the check
would fail on every rebuild and carry no information. The
rule this generalizes to is that verification hashes
computational outputs, not rendered artifacts, and it is
the same rule that governs the PDF in @sec-literate.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 4

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages: [check]

check:
  stage: check
  image: rocker/verse:4.4.0
  script:
    - make check
    - make docker-render-book
    - make check-renv
```

**The two structural differences.**

*Jobs and steps versus stages and scripts.* GitHub Actions
composes a job from reusable `uses:` steps, each a
versioned action maintained elsewhere, so the workflow
reads as an assembly of components. GitLab CI defines
stages containing jobs whose bodies are shell scripts, so
the pipeline reads as commands in an image. The GitHub
form is more declarative and depends on an ecosystem of
actions; the GitLab form is more direct and depends on
nothing but the image.

*Per-file versus single-file configuration.* GitHub reads
every file under `.github/workflows/`, so a project
naturally accumulates several workflows with separate
triggers. GitLab reads a single `.gitlab-ci.yml` at the
root, so everything is expressed in one file with rules
selecting what runs when.

**Why a Makefile shrinks both.** The differences above are
entirely about *orchestration*: what runs, in what order,
on what trigger. The check logic itself, run `R CMD check`,
render the report, verify the manifests, is identical in
both and belongs in neither file. Putting it behind named
targets leaves each CI file a thin shim naming the image
and calling a short list of them. The logic is then
single-sourced, testable locally with the same command CI
runs, and portable to a third forge for the cost of one
more shim. This is not a hypothetical convenience: a
zzcollab-scaffolded compendium's own `Makefile` already
ships `check` (`R CMD check --as-cran`, building first) and
`check-renv` (the dependency-manifest gate, run on the
host) as real targets, along with archetype-specific render
targets such as `docker-render-book` for a Quarto book, so
the two `.yml` files above can call them as written rather
than reimplementing the check logic inline. There is no
plain `make render` target; the render step's actual name
depends on the archetype (`docker-render-qmd` for a single
report, `docker-render-book` for a book, `docker-render` for
an `.Rmd` report), so a reader adapting this exercise to
their own compendium should name the target that matches
it, not assume `render` is a zzcollab convention.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 5

**Data analysis:** `R CMD check` and the manifest gate
always; the render gate if a report is produced.
**Manuscript:** all three, since the rendered document is
the deliverable. **R package:** `R CMD check` and the
manifest gate; the render gate only if a vignette exists.
**Simulation:** `R CMD check` and the manifest gate; the
render gate if a report is produced, plus a
seed-determinism check. **Blog:** the render gate above
all, since the deliverable is the site, with `R CMD check`
and the manifest gate applying to any code the posts run.

**Arranging the simulation.** CI runs a reduced pipeline:
the same driver, the same functions, the same seed, with
the replicate count set by a parameter to something small,
perhaps a hundred replicates in place of a hundred
thousand. The full pipeline runs elsewhere, on a cluster,
and its outputs are recorded and deposited.

**What the fixed seed contributes.** It is what makes the
reduced run a genuine reproducibility test rather than a
smoke test. With the seed fixed, the first hundred
replicates of the reduced run are *the same hundred
replicates* the full run begins with, so their summary is
a deterministic value that can be recorded and compared
exactly. Without the seed, the reduced run could only be
checked against a tolerance derived from Monte Carlo
error, which is a much weaker statement and one that
passes even when the generator has changed.

The honest limit: the reduced run verifies that the
machinery reproduces, not that the full study's estimates
are correct, since a hundred replicates estimate the
target quantity poorly. It tests the pipeline, not the
science.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 6

**The shared role.** Both are an independent re-execution
of the analysis in an environment the author does not
control, performed by a party who has no stake in it
succeeding. A CI runner does this for every committed
change, cheaply and mechanically; a codechecker does it
once for a submitted manuscript, expensively and with
judgment. In both cases the value comes from the same
property: the analysis runs somewhere that carries none of
the author's undeclared state, so anything the author
depended on without knowing it is exposed.

**What a human codechecker catches that the author's own
CI cannot.** The class of failure in which the CI
configuration itself encodes the author's assumptions. CI
is written by the author, so it tests what the author
thought to test, in an environment the author specified,
against outputs the author chose to compare. A workflow
that installs a system library the Dockerfile omits, or
that quietly skips the expensive analysis and checks only
the cheap one, or that compares against a baseline the
author generated after the bug was introduced, passes
indefinitely while the compendium is not reproducible at
all.

A codechecker reads the paper, forms an independent view
of what the analysis is supposed to produce, and checks
that the artifacts produce it. That is a judgment about
whether the right thing was verified, and no amount of
automation supplies it, because the automation is the
thing in question.

The compact statement: CI answers 'does the analysis still
do what it did', and a codechecker answers 'does the
analysis do what the paper says'.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 7

```r
used <- unique(renv::dependencies('R/cohort.R')$Package)
base_pkgs <- rownames(installed.packages(priority = 'base'))
missing <- setdiff(used, c('tibble', 'ggplot2', 'stats',
                            'utils', base_pkgs))
length(missing)   # 0
```

Against the real file, `used` is `tibble`, `stats`, and
`utils` (verified on R 4.6.1, `renv` from source, October
2026), every one of which is already in the pinned set
plus the base packages, so `missing` is a character vector
of length 0.

```r
# after appending `library(sandwich)` to a copy of R/cohort.R
used2 <- unique(renv::dependencies('cohort_copy.R')$Package)
missing2 <- setdiff(used2, c('tibble', 'ggplot2', 'stats',
                             'utils', base_pkgs))
missing2   # "sandwich"
```

`renv::dependencies()` finds the new `library(sandwich)`
call, and `missing2` is exactly `"sandwich"`, named and
nothing else, which is what a real CI log would print at
the dependency-manifest gate.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 8

A CI runner tests only what is checked out from version
control, which is exactly what is committed, no more. An
uncommitted change exists solely on the author's own
machine, so from the runner's point of view it does not
exist at all; the runner cannot fail on a problem it never
sees, and it cannot confirm a fix that was never pushed
either. 'Commit before you compute' is therefore not an
independent good habit sitting beside CI, it is what makes
CI's test meaningful in the first place: without it, a
green build certifies a state of the repository that
nobody's actual analysis ran against.

**A concrete example.** An analyst fixes a bug in
`analysis/scripts/02_model.R`, reruns the report locally,
confirms the figure now looks right, and pushes, but
forgets to `git add` a second file, a helper function in
`R/model_utils.R` the fix also depended on. Locally,
everything passes, because the uncommitted helper is still
on disk. On push, the runner checks out only what was
committed, the helper function is missing or stale, and the
render gate fails at the first chunk that calls it, a
failure the author cannot reproduce by looking at their own
unchanged working directory until they notice the file was
never staged.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Command or rule | What it does |
|---|---|
| `error-on: '"warning"'` (GitHub) / `error_on = "warning"` (`rcmdcheck`) | Fails `R CMD check` on any WARNING, including an undeclared import; `"error"` lets it through. |
| `zzrenvcheck::check_packages(strict = TRUE, error_on_fail = TRUE)` | Dependency-manifest gate; `error_on_fail = TRUE` is required to stop the step. |
| `renv::dependencies('analysis')` | Scans source for packages actually used; the core of a hand-written dependency gate. |
| `rmarkdown::render(...)` in a CI step | The render gate: fails the job if any chunk errors on a clean restore. |
| `docker build -t compendium:ci .` | Rebuilds the project image from a clean machine, the L2 rebuild `zzc verify --full` requires. |
| `test-baseline-*.R` naming | What `zzc verify --full` and `ci/run-tests.R` look for to certify L3. |
| `digest(x, algo = 'sha256')` | Checksums bytes that should not change (raw data); the wrong tool for a floating-point estimate. |
| `.Rbuildignore` entry for `analysis/` | Why `R CMD check` never sees analysis scripts or their dependencies. |
| Rule of thumb | Verify computational outputs within a tolerance; never hash rendered PDF or HTML bytes. |
| Habit 4 | Make every gate able to fail, and watch it fail once. |
| Habit 6 | Rebuild from clean, on a machine that is not yours. |

## Further reading

The distinction between capturing reproducibility and
validating it, which organizes this chapter, is drawn out
across the introduction of this book (@sec-intro) and rests
on the general framing of computational reproducibility as
a spectrum in @peng2011.

On independent, external verification, the CODECHECK
initiative described by Nust and Eglen
[@nust2021codecheck] is the most concrete model of
re-execution during peer review, and repays reading for its
account of what a codechecker does and does not certify.
The ACM's artifact review and badging policy [@acm2020]
documents the badge scheme now common at computing venues.

On the persistence of the problem that all this machinery
addresses, Stodden and colleagues [@stodden2018] analyze
the effectiveness of journal reproducibility policies and
find, soberingly, that a policy on paper is not a
reproduction in practice, and Trisovic and colleagues
[@trisovic2022], in re-running thousands of deposited R
files, quantify how often re-execution simply fails, which
is the empirical case for the standing checks this chapter
describes.

For the practices that surround the tooling, the ten simple
rules of Sandve and colleagues [@sandve2013] place
automated checking and independent re-execution among their
recommendations, and connect the mechanics of CI to the
habits that make it worthwhile.
